partText: (a) Define the radian.
B_keywords: [["angle"], ["arc", "distance along", "length"], ["radius"], ["equal", "same", "=", "equals"]]
modelAnswer: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
explanation: One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius of the circle (θ = arc length / radius).

partText:
(b)(i) Three children are playing on a roundabout (rotatable horizontal platform) at a playground. Child X is standing on the edge of the roundabout. This child is pushing so that the edge of the roundabout moves in a circle at a constant speed of ${vx} m s−1, as shown in the view from above in Figure 1.1.${f11}The radius of the roundabout is 3R.
Child Y is sitting on the roundabout at a distance 2R from the centre.
Child Z is sitting at a distance R from the centre.

Child Y is moving in a circle with an angular speed of ${w} rad s−1.

Calculate the radius of the roundabout.
modelAnswer: v = rω, so r = ${vx} / ${w} = ${rs} m
explanation: All the children on the roundabout have the same angular speed. Child X moves at speed v on a circle of radius 3R (the edge), so use v = rω with the angular speed.

partText: (b)(ii) Calculate the frequency of rotation of the roundabout.
modelAnswer: ω = 2πf, so f = ${w} / 2π = ${fs} Hz
explanation: Angular speed and frequency are related by ω = 2πf (one revolution is 2π rad).

partText: (b)(iii) Calculate the centripetal acceleration of child Y.
modelAnswer: child Y is at a distance 2R = (2/3) × ${rs} m from the centre; a = rω² = (2/3 × ${rs}) × ${w}² = ${as} m s⁻²
explanation: Centripetal acceleration a = rω², where r is the distance of Y from the centre (2R, which is two thirds of the radius 3R).

partText: (c) For the roundabout in 1(b), compare the linear and angular velocities for child X and child Z at any instant in time. For each row complete Table 1.1. For the magnitude type less, equal or greater (comparing X with Z); for the direction type same or opposite.
modelAnswer: linear velocity: X greater than Z in magnitude, opposite in direction; angular velocity: equal magnitude and same direction
explanation: Both children are on the same rigid roundabout, so they have the same angular velocity (equal magnitude, same direction). Linear velocity v = rω: X is at a greater radius so is faster. X and Z are on opposite sides of the centre, so their velocities point in opposite directions.
tableRowLabels: ["linear velocity: magnitude of X compared with Z","linear velocity: direction of X compared with Z","angular velocity: magnitude and direction of X compared with Z"]

partText: (a) Define electric field at a point.
B_keywords: force per unit positive charge|force per unit charge|force on unit positive charge|force per charge|force/charge|f/q|force exerted per unit positive charge|force acting per unit positive charge|force on a unit positive charge|force per positive charge|force per coulomb|force on a positive unit charge|force that acts on a unit positive charge|force on 1 c|force per unit +ve charge|force on a positive test charge per unit charge
modelAnswer: The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive charge acting on a stationary positive test charge at that point.
explanation: Electric field strength E = F / q: the force exerted per unit positive charge placed at the point.

partText:
(b)(i) An oil droplet has charge of magnitude Q. The droplet is held in equilibrium by the electric field between two horizontal parallel plates. The electric field is created by a potential difference (p.d.) V between the plates, with the lower plate at the ${hl} electric potential. The separation of the plates is x.

Which sketch shows four electric field lines that represent the electric field between the plates?
modelAnswer: Four straight, parallel, evenly spaced field lines perpendicular to the plates, each starting on one plate and finishing on the other, with arrows pointing ${fdir} (from the plate at the higher potential to the plate at the lower potential).
explanation: Between parallel plates the field is uniform: the lines are parallel, equally spaced and perpendicular to the plates. The direction is from the plate at the higher potential to the plate at the lower potential (the direction of the force on a positive charge).

partText: (b)(ii) Explain, with reference to forces, whether the sign of Q is positive or negative.
B_keywords: electric force is upwards|electric force upwards|electric force must be upwards|electric force acts upwards|electric force acts up|electric force is up|electric force up|upward electric force|upwards electric force|force is upwards|force upwards|upward force|upwards force|must act upwards|must be upwards|balances the weight|balance the weight|balances the gravitational|balances gravitational|opposes the weight|opposes weight|electric force opposes|cancels the weight|equal and opposite to the weight|equal to the weight|weight is downwards|gravitational force is downwards|weight acts downwards|weight downwards
modelAnswer: The weight (gravitational force) is downwards, so the electric force on the droplet must be upwards. The field is ${fdir}, so the electric force is ${sgn=="positive"?"in the same direction as":"opposite to"} the field and Q is ${sgn}.
explanation: For equilibrium the electric force balances the weight, so it acts upwards. A positive charge experiences a force in the direction of the field; a negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field. Here the field points ${fdir}, so Q is ${sgn}.

partText: (c)(i) For the oil droplet in 2(b), state an expression, in terms of some or all of Q, V and x, for the electric field strength E.
modelAnswer: E = V / x
explanation: In a uniform field the field strength is the potential difference divided by the plate separation.

partText: (c)(ii) State an expression, in terms of some or all of Q, V and x, for the weight W of the droplet.
modelAnswer: W = QV / x
explanation: The droplet is in equilibrium, so the weight equals the electric force, W = QE = QV/x.

partText:
(d) The plates in 2(b) have a p.d. across them of ${Vv} V and a separation of ${xx} m. The magnitude of the charge on the oil droplet is ${nq}e, where e is the elementary charge.

Calculate the mass of the oil droplet.
explanation: The weight of the droplet equals the electric force: mg = QE = QV/x with Q = ${nq}e.

partText:
(e) The polarity of the p.d. across the plates in 2(b) is reversed.

Describe and explain the subsequent motion of the oil droplet.
B_keywords: both forces now act downwards|both now act downwards|electric force now acts downwards|electric force is now acting downwards|both forces are acting downwards|both forces now downwards|electric force is now downwards|electric force now downwards|electric force downwards|electric force acts downwards|electric force is downwards|electric force is now down|both forces are downwards|both forces downwards|both forces act downwards|both forces are now downwards|force is now downwards|electric force reverses|electric force changes direction|field is reversed|field reverses|direction of the electric force reverses|force now acts downwards|electric force acts down
B2_keywords: accelerates downwards|accelerates downward|accelerates down|accelerate downwards|acceleration downwards|downward acceleration|moves downwards|moves downward|falls|falling|accelerates towards the lower plate|accelerates to the lower plate|moves down|will fall|drops|travels downwards
modelAnswer: The electric force now acts downwards (the same direction as the weight), so the resultant force is downwards and the droplet accelerates downwards.
explanation: Reversing the polarity reverses the field and so the electric force. Both the electric force and the weight now act downwards, so there is a resultant downward force and the droplet accelerates downwards (F = ma).

partText: (a) Define specific latent heat of fusion.
B_keywords: energy per unit mass|thermal energy per unit mass|heat per unit mass|energy per kg|per unit mass|per kilogram|energy per mass|energy required per unit mass|energy/mass|q/m|l=q/m|energy per 1 kg|energy needed per unit mass|heat required per unit mass|thermal energy required per unit mass|thermal energy per kilogram
B2_keywords: [["solid", "melt", "fusion", "freez", "ice"], ["liquid", "change of state", "change state", "changing state", "phase", "without change in temperature", "constant temperature", "no change in temperature", "same temperature", "without a change in temperature", "without changing temperature", "without temperature change", "no temperature change"]]
modelAnswer: The (thermal) energy required per unit mass to change a substance from solid to liquid (change of state) without a change in temperature.
explanation: Specific latent heat of fusion L = Q / m: the thermal energy per unit mass needed to melt a solid at constant temperature (the melting point).

partText: (b) Explain why substances usually have a higher specific latent heat for vaporisation than for fusion.
B_keywords: change in volume is greater|volume change is greater|greater change in volume|larger change in volume|bigger change in volume|greater volume change|larger volume change|volume increases more|expands more|greater expansion|more expansion|increase in volume is greater|volume increase is greater|volume changes more|greater increase in volume|larger increase in volume|change in volume is larger|change in volume is bigger|greater increase in the volume|larger increase in the volume|bigger increase in volume|much larger volume|much greater volume
modelAnswer: The change in volume is greater for vaporisation than for fusion, so more work is done against the atmosphere (so more thermal energy must be supplied).
explanation: When a liquid vaporises its volume increases enormously. The expanding vapour does work pushing back the atmosphere, so extra thermal energy is needed in addition to that required to separate the molecules.

partText:
(c) An ice cube of mass ${mi} g at a temperature of −${Ti} °C is removed from a freezer. The ice cube is immediately placed in an insulated beaker that contains a mass of ${mw} g of water at a temperature of ${Tw} °C.

The specific heat capacity of water is 4.19 kJ kg−1 °C−1.
The specific heat capacity of ice is 2.11 kJ kg−1 °C−1.
The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 336 kJ kg−1.
The beaker has negligible specific heat capacity.

The contents of the beaker are left to reach thermal equilibrium.

Calculate the temperature, in °C, of the water in the beaker when thermal equilibrium is reached.
modelAnswer: energy lost by the water = energy gained by the ice: ${mw} × 4.19 × (${Tw} − θ) = ${mi} × 2.11 × ${Ti} + ${mi} × 336 + ${mi} × 4.19 × θ, so θ = ${ths} °C
explanation: Energy lost by the cooling water = energy to warm the ice to 0 °C + energy to melt the ice + energy to warm the melted ice from 0 °C to the final temperature θ. Use Q = mcΔθ for each warming stage and Q = mL for melting. The masses may be left in grams because the same unit appears on both sides.

partText:
The first law of thermodynamics may be written as

ΔU = Q + W

where W is the work done on a system.

(a) State the meaning, in this equation, of the symbols ΔU and Q.
B_keywords: increase in internal energy|change in internal energy|increase in the internal energy|change in the internal energy|increase of internal energy|change of internal energy|internal energy increase|internal energy change|increase in total internal energy|increase in energy of the system|increase in the internal energy of the system
B2_keywords: thermal energy transferred to the system|thermal energy supplied to the system|thermal energy added to the system|heat transferred to the system|heat supplied to the system|heat added to the system|energy transferred to the system by heating|thermal energy transferred to|thermal energy supplied to|thermal energy added to|heat transferred to|heat supplied to|heat added to|heat energy supplied|heat energy added|heat energy transferred to|energy supplied by heating|heat flow into the system|heat into the system|thermal energy into the system|energy transferred to the system as heat|thermal energy gained by the system|heat gained by the system|heat given to the system|thermal energy given to the system|heat absorbed by the system|thermal energy absorbed by the system|energy transferred as heat to the system|energy transferred thermally to the system
modelAnswer: ΔU is the increase in internal energy of the system. Q is the thermal energy transferred to (supplied to) the system.
explanation: In ΔU = Q + W, ΔU is the increase in the internal energy of the system, Q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

partText:
(b)(i) An ideal gas at a pressure of ${p} × 105 Pa has an initial volume of ${V1} m3, an initial thermodynamic temperature of ${T1} K, and an initial internal energy of ${U1} kJ.
The volume of the gas is reduced at constant pressure to a final volume of ${V2} m3.

Show that the magnitude of the work done on the gas is ${Wv} J.
explanation: At constant pressure the work done is W = pΔV, where ΔV is the magnitude of the change in volume.

partText: (b)(ii) Explain whether the work done on the gas is positive or negative.
B_keywords: [["positive", "+ve", "+"], ["compress", "volume decreas", "volume is reduced", "volume reduc", "reduction in volume", "decrease in volume", "done on", "volume gets smaller", "volume is smaller", "volume gets less", "volume of the gas decreases", "smaller volume", "pushed in", "squash", "less volume", "gas is being compressed"]]
modelAnswer: The work done on the gas is positive because the gas is compressed (its volume decreases).
explanation: W in ΔU = Q + W is the work done on the gas. The volume decreases, so the surroundings do work on the gas and W is positive.

partText: (b)(iii) Explain why the final internal energy of the gas is ${U2} kJ.
B_keywords: [["volume", "v∝", "v/t", "charles", "v is proportional", "v proportional", "v directly"], ["proportional", "∝", "directly", "v/t", "pv/t", "charles", "linear", "constant pressure"]]
B2_keywords: [["proportional", "∝", "directly", "depends on", "depend on", "function of", "linked to", "related to", "dependent on"], ["internal energy", "energy", "u∝", "u=", "u is"]]
modelAnswer: At constant pressure the volume V ∝ T. The volume has been reduced to one ${kwn} of its initial value, so T has also been reduced to one ${kwn}. The internal energy U ∝ T, so U is also reduced to one ${kwn}: ${U1} / ${k} = ${U2} kJ.
explanation: For an ideal gas at constant pressure V ∝ T, so T falls by the same factor as V (from ${T1} K to ${T2} K). The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the random kinetic energies of the molecules, which is proportional to T, so U falls by the same factor: ${U1} / ${k} = ${U2} kJ.

partText: (c) For the reduction of the volume of the gas in 4(b), calculate Q. Give a unit with your answer.
modelAnswer: ΔU = ${U2} − ${U1} = ${dUk} kJ = ${dU} J; Q = ΔU − W = ${dU} − ${Wv} = ${Qj} J = ${Qk} kJ
explanation: The change in internal energy is ΔU = final − initial = ${dUk} kJ. From ΔU = Q + W with W = +${Wv} J, Q = ΔU − W. The negative sign shows that thermal energy is transferred from the gas to the surroundings.

partText: (a) State what is represented by the Avogadro constant.
B_keywords: [["number", "atoms", "particles", "molecules", "entities"], ["per mole", "in one mole", "in a mole", "in 1 mole", "in 12 g", "in 12g", "in 0.012 kg", "in 1 mol", "in one mol", "each mole", "every mole", "permole"]]
modelAnswer: The number of particles (atoms or molecules) per mole (in one mole of a substance).
explanation: The Avogadro constant N_A is the number of particles (atoms or molecules) in one mole of a substance.

partText:
(b) A gas is in a sealed container that has a fixed volume. The thermodynamic temperature T of the gas is varied.
Figure 5.1 shows how the pressure p of the gas varies with NT, where N is the number of molecules of the gas.
Figure 5.2 shows how the mean-square speed ⟨c2⟩ of the molecules of the gas varies with T.
Figure 5.3 shows how the total kinetic energy EK of all the molecules of the gas varies with T.${f5}Determine three conclusions about the gas that can be drawn from Figure 5.1, Figure 5.2 and Figure 5.3. The conclusions may be qualitative or quantitative. Use the space below for any working.
A_keywords: ideal|p∝nt|p∝t|proportional to nt|proportional to t|pv=nkt|pv=nrt|obeys the ideal gas|obeys pv|follows pv|obeys the gas laws|obeys boyle|obeys charles|obeys the pressure law
B_keywords: ${Vk}
modelAnswer: Any three of: the gas is ideal (p ∝ NT, ⟨c²⟩ ∝ T and E_K ∝ T are straight lines through the origin); the volume of the container is ${Vk} m³ (from the gradient of Figure 5.1, V = k/gradient); the mass of one molecule is ${mk} kg (m = 3kT/⟨c²⟩ ≈ molar mass ${Mkg} kg mol⁻¹, so the gas is ${gname}); the number of molecules is ${Nk} (E_K = 3/2 NkT), which is ${nk} mol; the mass of gas is ${gmk} kg (or the density is ${rhok} kg m⁻³).
explanation: The three graphs are all straight lines through the origin, so p ∝ NT, ⟨c²⟩ ∝ T and E_K ∝ T, which is ideal-gas behaviour. Quantitative conclusions: V = k/(gradient of Fig 5.1) = ${Vk} m³; m = 3kT/⟨c²⟩ = ${mk} kg; N = 2E_K/(3kT) = ${Nk}, so n = N/N_A = ${nk} mol; mass of gas = Nm = ${gmk} kg.

partText:
(c)(i) One assumption of the kinetic theory of gases is that the volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.

State, with a reason, whether this assumption applies to the gas in 5(b).
B_keywords: [["yes", "applies", "does apply", "assumption is valid", "is valid", "true", "correct"], ["ideal", "proportional", "straight line", "obeys pv", "follows pv", "linear"]]

explanation: The graphs show the gas obeys the ideal gas equation, and an ideal gas is one for which the kinetic-theory assumptions (including negligible molecular volume) hold, so the assumption applies.

partText: (c)(ii) State two other assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.

partText: (a) State what is meant by simple harmonic motion.
B_keywords: [["acceleration", "a∝", "force"], ["proportional", "∝", "directly"], ["displacement", "distance", "x", "equilibrium", "fixed point"]]
B2_keywords: opposite direction|opposite in direction|directed towards|towards a fixed point|towards the equilibrium|towards equilibrium|towards the centre|towards the mean position|towards the central point|opposite to displacement|opposite to the displacement|negative|a=-|a=−|a=–|−ω²x|-ω²x|–ω²x|-ω^2|−ω^2|–ω^2|directed to a fixed point|directed towards a fixed point|directed towards the equilibrium|always towards the equilibrium|always towards a fixed point|acts towards|always opposite|oppositeto
modelAnswer: The acceleration of the oscillating object is proportional to its displacement from a fixed (equilibrium) point and is always directed towards that point (opposite in direction to the displacement).
explanation: Simple harmonic motion: a ∝ −x, i.e. the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and is in the opposite direction to the displacement (towards a fixed point).

partText:
(b)(i) A length of thick copper wire is formed into a rectangular frame, as shown in Figure 6.1.${f61}The frame has side lengths of ${H} cm and ${Wd} cm.
There is a small gap XY at the ends of the wire at the top of the frame.
The frame is suspended so that it hangs vertically using thin cotton thread attached to the two ends of the wire. The frame oscillates about its vertical axis, as shown in the view from above in Figure 6.2.${f62}The oscillations are simple harmonic. The displacement s of the edge of the frame from its equilibrium position varies with time t according to

s = ${A} sin ${w}t

where s is in mm and t is in s.

Calculate the period T of the oscillations.
modelAnswer: ω = 2π / T, so T = 2π / ${w} = ${Ts} s
explanation: Compare s = A sin ωt with s = ${A} sin ${w}t: the angular frequency ω = ${w} rad s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π/ω.

partText: (b)(ii) Show that the maximum speed of the edges of the frame is ${v02} mm s−1.
explanation: In simple harmonic motion the maximum speed is v₀ = ωx₀, where x₀ = ${A} mm is the amplitude and ω = ${w} rad s⁻¹. (Differentiating s = ${A} sin ${w}t gives v = ${A} × ${w} cos ${w}t.)

partText:
(c)(i) The frame in 6(b) is in a uniform horizontal magnetic field that is parallel to the equilibrium position of the frame.
The flux density of the magnetic field is ${B} T.

Calculate the electromotive force (e.m.f.) E0 induced across XY when the frame is moving at its maximum speed.
modelAnswer: E = BLv for each vertical edge; there are two edges moving across the field, so E₀ = B × 2L × v₀ = ${B} × ${H2m} × (${v02} × 10⁻³) = ${E02} V
explanation: The e.m.f. is the rate of change of flux linkage: E = BLv for each moving vertical edge (length L = ${Hm} m). Both vertical edges cut flux in the same sense, so the e.m.f. across XY is E₀ = B(2L)v₀ with v₀ = ${v02} × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹. The width of the frame is not needed.

partText: (c)(ii) Which sketch shows the variation of the induced e.m.f. E across XY with t between t = 0 and t = 2T?
modelAnswer: A cosine curve of amplitude E₀ that starts at E₀ at t = 0, crosses zero at T/4, 3T/4, 5T/4 and 7T/4 and completes two full cycles by t = 2T.
explanation: The displacement is s = A sin ωt, so the velocity v = Aω cos ωt. The e.m.f. is proportional to the speed of the edges, so E = E₀ cos ωt: it is a maximum at t = 0, T, 2T and zero at T/4, 3T/4, 5T/4 and 7T/4.

partText: (a) State what is meant by the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current.
A_keywords: same power|same mean power|same average power|same heating|same heating effect|same energy|same rate of energy|same thermal energy|same rate of heating|same power dissipation|same power dissipated|same mean rate|same rate of dissipation|equal power|equal heating|equal mean power|same effect|same average rate|mean of the squares|mean square|average of the square|mean of the square|mean of square|mean value of the square|average value of the square|mean of squares
M_keywords: direct current|steady current|constant current|d.c.|dc current|d.c. current|steady d.c.|constant d.c.|direct|steady|constant|square root of the mean|square root of the average|root of the mean of the square|square root of mean
modelAnswer: The r.m.s. current is the value of the direct (steady) current that dissipates the same mean power in a resistor as the alternating current.
explanation: r.m.s. current: the steady (direct) current that would dissipate the same mean power in a given resistor as the alternating current does.

partText: (b)(i) There is a sinusoidal alternating current in a resistor of resistance ${R} Ω. The power P dissipated in the resistor varies with time t as shown in Figure 7.1.${f71}Determine the mean power dissipated in the resistor.
modelAnswer: The graph oscillates between 0 and ${Pmax} W, so the mean power = ${Pmax} / 2 = ${Pms} W
explanation: Over a whole number of cycles the power varies symmetrically between 0 and its peak value ${Pmax} W, so the mean power is half the peak power.

partText: (b)(ii) Calculate the r.m.s. current in the resistor.
modelAnswer: P = I²R, so I = √(${Pms} / ${R}) = ${Is} A
explanation: The mean power is P = I_rms²R, so I_rms = √(P/R) using the mean power from (b)(i).

partText:
(c)(i) The current in the resistor in 7(b) is now half-wave rectified.

State the name of the electric circuit component that is used to achieve this rectification.
B_keywords: diode|semiconductor diode|rectifier diode|p-n junction|p−n junction|p–n junction|pn junction|p-n diode|p−n diode|p–n diode|rectifying diode
modelAnswer: A diode.
explanation: A diode conducts in one direction only, so it removes one half of each cycle of the alternating current.

partText: (c)(ii) Which sketch shows the variation of the power P dissipated in the resistor between t = 0 and t = ${T0s} s?
modelAnswer: The power follows the same cos² shape as in Figure 7.1, with a maximum of ${Pmax} W, but it is zero for the middle half of the time (from ${T0s}/4 to 3×${T0s}/4) while the diode blocks the current.
explanation: With half-wave rectification the current is zero for half of each cycle, so the power is zero for that half. During the conducting half the power is unchanged: P = I²R follows the same cos² curve with the same maximum ${Pmax} W.

partText: (c)(iii) Determine the r.m.s. current in the resistor. Explain your reasoning.
B_keywords: [["power", "p", "energy", "heating"], ["half", "halved", "halves", "1/2", "0.5", "50%", "half the time", "half of the time", "half the cycle", "half of the cycle", "zero for half", "reduced by a factor of 2", "factor of 2", "factor 2", "divided by 2", "÷2"]]
modelAnswer: The mean power is halved (the current is zero for half of the time), so the mean power = ${Pm3s} W and I_rms = √(${Pm3s} / ${R}) = ${Is2} A
explanation: The power is zero for half of each cycle and unchanged for the other half, so the mean power halves to ${Pm3s} W. Then I_rms = √(P/R) = √(${Pm3s} / ${R}) = ${Is2} A.

partText:
A star in a distant galaxy consists mostly of hydrogen. Visible light emitted by the star consists of discrete spectral absorption lines at wavelengths of 410 nm, 434 nm, 486 nm and 656 nm.

(a) Explain, with reference to photons, how the existence of these spectral lines provides evidence for discrete electron energy levels in the hydrogen atom.
B_keywords: [["difference", "change", "transition", "jump", "drop", "falls", "moves between", "moving between", "moves from", "e=hf", "hf=", "e2−e1", "e2-e1", "Δe", "between energy levels", "between levels"], ["energy level", "energy levels", "levels", "electron", "state", "states"]]
B2_keywords: [["wavelength", "wavelengths", "frequency", "frequencies", "lines"], ["energy difference", "energy change", "energy transition", "energy gap", "energy of photon", "energy of the photon", "energies of photons", "energies of the photons", "photon energy", "photon energies", "energy of each photon", "energies", "energy"]]
modelAnswer: Any three of: photons have discrete (specific) energies; the photon energy is equal to the difference between two electron energy levels; discrete wavelengths mean discrete photon energies, so only certain energy differences are possible; therefore the electron energy levels are discrete.
explanation: A photon carries energy E = hf = hc/λ. Each spectral line is one wavelength, so one photon energy. A photon is absorbed when an electron makes a transition between two energy levels, so the photon energy equals the difference between the levels. Only a few discrete wavelengths are seen, so only certain energy differences exist, which shows that the energy levels are discrete.
B3_keywords: [["electron", "electrons", "energy level", "energy levels", "levels", "atom"], ["discrete", "fixed", "quantised", "quantized", "specific energies", "specific energy", "only certain", "only particular"]]

partText:
